questions.q: What is the main problem with writing all business logic directly inside the trigger body?
options: It's hard to test and reuse, since a trigger itself can't be called from elsewhere
Triggers cannot contain for loops
Triggers are limited to 10 lines of code
Trigger.new becomes read-only once logic is added
questions.explain: Logic sitting directly in a trigger body can't be invoked or unit tested in isolation the way an ordinary class method can.

questions.q: In the handler pattern, what should the trigger body itself contain?
options: All of the field validation logic
Only the DML statements
Just enough code to route to the appropriate handler method based on context
A copy of every SOQL query used by the handler
questions.explain: A 'thin' trigger only checks the context (e.g. Trigger.isBefore && Trigger.isInsert) and calls the matching handler method — the handler class holds the actual logic.

questions.q: Why is it valuable to give each trigger event its own handler method (beforeInsert, afterUpdate, etc.) rather than one large method with nested ifs?
options: Salesforce requires a separate method per event
It's purely a naming convention with no practical benefit
Multiple methods run faster than a single method
Each method stays focused on one job and is easier to find and maintain
questions.explain: Splitting by context keeps each method's responsibility clear, which scales much better as logic grows.

questions.q: What does a shared trigger framework base class typically provide beyond a single hand-rolled handler?
options: Automatic translation of Apex into other languages
A reusable routing/dispatch mechanism and a place to add cross-cutting concerns like recursion guards, shared by every trigger that uses it
The ability to skip writing any Apex code at all
Guaranteed execution order across unrelated objects
questions.explain: A framework's base class standardizes how context is detected and dispatched, so features like a recursion guard only need to be written once and every handler extending it benefits.

questions.q: Why can `handler.beforeInsert(someList)` be unit tested without needing real DML, where the equivalent logic directly inside the trigger body cannot?
options: Handler methods always return a value, while triggers never do
A handler is an ordinary class method you can call directly with an in-memory list, bypassing the DML required to actually fire a trigger
Test classes cannot contain trigger-related code at all
Handler methods are automatically mocked by the testing framework
questions.explain: Because the handler is a plain class, a test can construct a list of sObjects in memory and call the method directly, without needing to insert/update real records to make the trigger fire.
